claim: In 1983, Akinori Noma made the first recordings of ATP-dependent potassium channels in rat cardiac myocytes.
source: In 1983, Akinori Noma made the first recordings of ATP-dependent potassium channels in rat cardiac myocytes (Noma, 1983).
evidence: Supported by citation to Noma, 1983

claim: ATP-dependent K+-channels spontaneously open in electrolyte solutions devoid of nucleotides in membrane patches excised from cardiac myocytes.
source: In membrane patches excised from cardiac myocytes, ATP-dependent K+-channels spontaneously open in electrolyte solutions devoid of nucleotides.
evidence: Supported by citation to Noma, 1983 in the same paragraph

claim: When exposed to milimolar concentrations of intracellular ATP, ATP-dependent K+-channels become quiescent.
source: When exposed to milimolar concentrations of intracellular ATP, these channels become quiescent.
evidence: Supported by citation to Noma, 1983 in the same paragraph

claim: Once ATP is removed, potassium currents re-emerge in ATP-dependent K+-channels.
source: Once ATP is removed, the potassium currents re-emerge, thus ATP facilitates channel closure.
evidence: Supported by citation to Noma, 1983 in the same paragraph

claim: KATP channels have been discovered in pancreatic beta cells.
source: KATP channels, as they are known, have since been discovered in other cells, including pancreatic beta cells (Cook and Hales, 1984)
evidence: Supported by citation to Cook and Hales, 1984

claim: KATP channels have been discovered in skeletal muscle fibers.
source: KATP channels, as they are known, have since been discovered in other cells, including pancreatic beta cells (Cook and Hales, 1984), skeletal (Spruce et al., 1985)
evidence: Supported by citation to Spruce et al., 1985

claim: KATP channels have been discovered in smooth muscle fibers.
source: KATP channels, as they are known, have since been discovered in other cells, including pancreatic beta cells (Cook and Hales, 1984), skeletal (Spruce et al., 1985) and smooth muscle (Standen et al., 1989) fibers
evidence: Supported by citation to Standen et al., 1989

claim: KATP channels have been discovered in neurons.
source: KATP channels, as they are known, have since been discovered in other cells, including pancreatic beta cells (Cook and Hales, 1984), skeletal (Spruce et al., 1985) and smooth muscle (Standen et al., 1989) fibers and neurons (Karschin et al., 1997; Nelson et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to Karschin et al., 1997 and Nelson et al., 2015

claim: Through their selectivity for K+ ions, KATP channels return membrane voltage toward the resting (Nernst K+) potential.
source: Through their selectivity for K+ ions KATP channels return membrane voltage toward the resting (Nernst K+) potential (Hibino et al., 2010; Hille, 2001).
evidence: Supported by citations to Hibino et al., 2010 and Hille, 2001

claim: Mg2+-ADP overrides ATP inhibition of KATP channels.
source: Mg2+-ADP overrides ATP inhibition (Dunne and Petersen, 1986; Kakei et al., 1986; Larsson et al., 1993; Nichols et al., 1996)
evidence: Supported by citations to Dunne and Petersen, 1986; Kakei et al., 1986; Larsson et al., 1993; Nichols et al., 1996

claim: Phosphatidyl-inositol diphosphate (PIP2) is required for KATP channel activity.
source: phosphatidyl-inositol diphosphate (PIP2) is required for activity (Baukrowitz et al., 1998; Hilgemann and Ball, 1996; Shyng and Nichols, 1998).
evidence: Supported by citations to Baukrowitz et al., 1998; Hilgemann and Ball, 1996; Shyng and Nichols, 1998

claim: KATP channels are thought to couple cellular metabolism to membrane excitability by virtue of their sensitivity to both ATP and ADP.
source: By virtue of their sensitivity to both ATP and ADP, these channels are thought to couple cellular metabolism to membrane excitability.
evidence: Based on inference from the described sensitivity to ATP and ADP

claim: Mutations in KATP channels are associated with congenital hyperinsulinism.
source: The physiological importance of KATP channels is underscored by mutations associated with heritable human diseases including congenital hyperinsulinism (Pinney et al., 2008; Saint-Martin et al., 2011; Sharma et al., 2000)
evidence: Supported by citations to Pinney et al., 2008; Saint-Martin et al., 2011; Sharma et al., 2000

claim: Mutations in KATP channels are associated with permanent neonatal diabetes mellitus.
source: The physiological importance of KATP channels is underscored by mutations associated with heritable human diseases including congenital hyperinsulinism (Pinney et al., 2008; Saint-Martin et al., 2011; Sharma et al., 2000) and permanent neonatal diabetes mellitus (Aittoniemi et al., 2009; Ashcroft et al., 2017; Letha et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citations to Aittoniemi et al., 2009; Ashcroft et al., 2017; Letha et al., 2007

claim: Drugs used in the treatment of diabetes mellitus target KATP channels.
source: Furthermore, drugs used in the treatment of diabetes mellitis, hypertension and alopecia target KATP channels (Aziz et al., 2014; Feldman, 1985; Rubaiy, 2016; Shorter et al., 2008; Standen et al., 1989; Sturgess et al., 1985).
evidence: Supported by citations to Aziz et al., 2014; Feldman, 1985; Rubaiy, 2016; Shorter et al., 2008; Standen et al., 1989; Sturgess et al., 1985

claim: Drugs used in the treatment of hypertension target KATP channels.
source: Furthermore, drugs used in the treatment of diabetes mellitis, hypertension and alopecia target KATP channels (Aziz et al., 2014; Feldman, 1985; Rubaiy, 2016; Shorter et al., 2008; Standen et al., 1989; Sturgess et al., 1985).
evidence: Supported by citations to Aziz et al., 2014; Feldman, 1985; Rubaiy, 2016; Shorter et al., 2008; Standen et al., 1989; Sturgess et al., 1985

claim: Drugs used in the treatment of alopecia target KATP channels.
source: Furthermore, drugs used in the treatment of diabetes mellitis, hypertension and alopecia target KATP channels (Aziz et al., 2014; Feldman, 1985; Rubaiy, 2016; Shorter et al., 2008; Standen et al., 1989; Sturgess et al., 1985).
evidence: Supported by citations to Aziz et al., 2014; Feldman, 1985; Rubaiy, 2016; Shorter et al., 2008; Standen et al., 1989; Sturgess et al., 1985

claim: KATP channels are large oligomeric complexes composed of four sulphonylurea receptor (SUR) subunits and four Kir6 subunits.
source: These channels were found to be large oligomeric complexes composed of four sulphonylurea receptor (SUR) subunits, which belong to the ABCC family of ABC transporters, and four Kir6 subunits, which are members of the inward rectifier potassium channel family (Clement et al., 1997; Inagaki et al., 1997; Shyng and Nichols, 1997).
evidence: Supported by citations to Clement et al., 1997; Inagaki et al., 1997; Shyng and Nichols, 1997

claim: SUR subunits belong to the ABCC family of ABC transporters.
source: These channels were found to be large oligomeric complexes composed of four sulphonylurea receptor (SUR) subunits, which belong to the ABCC family of ABC transporters, and four Kir6 subunits, which are members of the inward rectifier potassium channel family (Clement et al., 1997; Inagaki et al., 1997; Shyng and Nichols, 1997).
evidence: Supported by citations to Clement et al., 1997; Inagaki et al., 1997; Shyng and Nichols, 1997

claim: Kir6 subunits are members of the inward rectifier potassium channel family.
source: These channels were found to be large oligomeric complexes composed of four sulphonylurea receptor (SUR) subunits, which belong to the ABCC family of ABC transporters, and four Kir6 subunits, which are members of the inward rectifier potassium channel family (Clement et al., 1997; Inagaki et al., 1997; Shyng and Nichols, 1997).
evidence: Supported by citations to Clement et al., 1997; Inagaki et al., 1997; Shyng and Nichols, 1997

claim: Recent cryo-EM structures of hamster SUR1-mouse/rat Kir6.2 hybrid complexes presented the architecture of KATP, revealing a central K+ channel surrounded by four SURs.
source: Recent cryo-EM structures of hamster SUR1-mouse/rat Kir6.2 hybrid complexes presented the architecture of KATP, revealing a central K+ channel surrounded by four SURs (Li et al., 2017; Martin et al., 2017a, 2017b).
evidence: Supported by citations to Li et al., 2017; Martin et al., 2017a, 2017b

claim: In previous cryo-EM structures of KATP, the SURs extended away from the channel, akin to propellers.
source: The SURs extended away from the channel, akin to propellers, and their nucleotide-binding domains (NBDs) were empty and dissociated from each other.
evidence: Supported by citations to Li et al., 2017; Martin et al., 2017a, 2017b in the same paragraph

claim: In previous cryo-EM structures of KATP, the nucleotide-binding domains (NBDs) of SUR were empty and dissociated from each other.
source: The SURs extended away from the channel, akin to propellers, and their nucleotide-binding domains (NBDs) were empty and dissociated from each other.
evidence: Supported by citations to Li et al., 2017; Martin et al., 2017a, 2017b in the same paragraph

claim: In humans, there are two SUR genes (SUR1 and SUR2).
source: In humans, there are two SUR genes (SUR1 and SUR2) and two Kir6 genes (Kir6.2 and Kir6.1) (Aguilar-Bryan et al., 1995; Babenko et al., 1998; Chutkow et al., 1996; Inagaki et al., 1995a, Inagaki et al., 1995b, Inagaki et al., 1995c).
evidence: Supported by citations to Aguilar-Bryan et al., 1995; Babenko et al., 1998; Chutkow et al., 1996; Inagaki et al., 1995a, Inagaki et al., 1995b, Inagaki et al., 1995c

claim: In humans, there are two Kir6 genes (Kir6.2 and Kir6.1).
source: In humans, there are two SUR genes (SUR1 and SUR2) and two Kir6 genes (Kir6.2 and Kir6.1) (Aguilar-Bryan et al., 1995; Babenko et al., 1998; Chutkow et al., 1996; Inagaki et al., 1995a, Inagaki et al., 1995b, Inagaki et al., 1995c).
evidence: Supported by citations to Aguilar-Bryan et al., 1995; Babenko et al., 1998; Chutkow et al., 1996; Inagaki et al., 1995a, Inagaki et al., 1995b, Inagaki et al., 1995c

claim: The human KATP channel composed of SUR1 and Kir6.2 is found in pancreatic beta cells.
source: The focus of this study is the human KATP channel composed of SUR1 and Kir6.2, which are found in pancreatic beta cells where they play a major role in regulating insulin secretion.
evidence: Based on established scientific knowledge

claim: The human KATP channel composed of SUR1 and Kir6.2 plays a major role in regulating insulin secretion.
source: The focus of this study is the human KATP channel composed of SUR1 and Kir6.2, which are found in pancreatic beta cells where they play a major role in regulating insulin secretion.
evidence: Based on established scientific knowledge

claim: A six-amino acid linker containing three repeats of the Ser-Ala dyad was used to fuse the C-terminus of SUR1 to the N-terminus of Kir6.2.
source: To facilitate large-scale expression and purification of the human SUR1-Kir6.2 complex, we fused the C-terminus of SUR1 to the N-terminus of Kir6.2 using a six-amino acid linker containing three repeats of the Ser-Ala dyad.
evidence: Describes the experimental design used in this study

claim: Peptide linkers ranging from 6 to 14 residues have been used to generate KATP channel fusions that reproduce the electrophysiological and pharmacological characteristics of wild-type octameric KATP channels.
source: This and other peptide linkers ranging from 6 to 14 residues have been used to generate KATP channel fusions that reproduce the electrophysiological and pharmacological characteristics of wild-type octameric KATP channels, as assessed by inhibition from ATP and sulphonylurea drugs as well as activation by ADP and diazoxide (Chan et al., 2008; Clement et al., 1997; Mikhailov et al., 2005, 1998).
evidence: Supported by citations to Chan et al., 2008; Clement et al., 1997; Mikhailov et al., 2005, 1998

claim: Functional expression of the KATPem fusion construct was confirmed in electrophysiology recordings and ATPase measurements.
source: We also confirmed functional expression of our fusion construct (KATPem) in electrophysiology recordings and ATPase measurements (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1

claim: Cryo-EM reconstructions revealed two major conformations of KATPem.
source: Cryo-EM reconstructions revealed two major conformations (Figure 1A).
evidence: Supported by cryo-EM data shown in Figure 1A

claim: One conformation of KATPem is similar to the published 'propeller' form with the exception that the NBDs are closed.
source: One is similar to the published structure ('propeller' form) with the exception that the NBDs are closed in our structure (Figure 1C).
evidence: Supported by structural comparison with published structures and cryo-EM data shown in Figure 1C

claim: The other conformation of KATPem is referred to as the quatrefoil form and is dramatically different from the propeller form.
source: The other conformation, which we refer to as the quatrefoil form, is dramatically different (Figure 1B).
evidence: Supported by cryo-EM data shown in Figure 1B

claim: The NBDs are closed in the quatrefoil form.
source: The NBDs are also closed in the quatrefoil form; however, the SUR1 subunits reside in a different location relative to Kir6 (Figure 1B and C).
evidence: Supported by cryo-EM data shown in Figure 1B and C

claim: In the quatrefoil form, the SUR1 subunits reside in a different location relative to Kir6 compared to the propeller form.
source: The NBDs are also closed in the quatrefoil form; however, the SUR1 subunits reside in a different location relative to Kir6 (Figure 1B and C).
evidence: Supported by cryo-EM data shown in Figure 1B and C

claim: The propeller form was determined to 5.6 Å resolution.
source: Upon further classification and refinement, the propeller form was determined to 5.6 Å resolution and the quatrefoil form was determined to 3.9 Å resolution.
evidence: Supported by cryo-EM data processing and resolution determination

claim: The quatrefoil form was determined to 3.9 Å resolution.
source: Upon further classification and refinement, the propeller form was determined to 5.6 Å resolution and the quatrefoil form was determined to 3.9 Å resolution.
evidence: Supported by cryo-EM data processing and resolution determination

claim: The EM map of the quatrefoil form enabled building of 1596 out of 1977 residues in the complex and assignment of the amino acid register.
source: This enabled building of 1596 out of 1977 residues in the complex and assignment of the amino acid register (Figure 2).
evidence: Supported by model building from cryo-EM data

claim: The quatrefoil form EM map was of sufficient quality to identify ligands including Mg2+, ATP, and ADP.
source: In addition, the map was of sufficient quality to identify ligands including Mg2+, ATP, and ADP.
evidence: Supported by cryo-EM density map quality

claim: In the quatrefoil form, KATP is a symmetrical tetramer.
source: In the quatrefoil form, KATP is a symmetrical tetramer; each protomer consists of one K+ channel subunit and one ABC transporter.
evidence: Supported by structural analysis of cryo-EM data

claim: Each protomer in the quatrefoil form consists of one K+ channel subunit and one ABC transporter.
source: In the quatrefoil form, KATP is a symmetrical tetramer; each protomer consists of one K+ channel subunit and one ABC transporter.
evidence: Supported by structural analysis of cryo-EM data

claim: The ABC transporter in KATP has five domains: TMD0, TMD1, NBD1, TMD2 and NBD2.
source: There are five domains in the ABC transporter, TMD0, TMD1, NBD1, TMD2 and NBD2 (Figure 2A).
evidence: Supported by structural analysis shown in Figure 2A

claim: TMD1, NBD1, TMD2 and NBD2 form the transporter module.
source: The latter four domains form the transporter module.
evidence: Supported by structural analysis

claim: The K+ channel consists of a transmembrane domain and a cytoplasmic domain (CTD).
source: The K+ channel consists of a transmembrane domain and a cytoplasmic domain (CTD), which form the ion pathway through the complex (Figure 2B).
evidence: Supported by structural analysis shown in Figure 2B

claim: At the molecular center of the quatrefoil form, the four subunits of Kir6.2 form a canonical inward-rectifier K+ channel structure.
source: At the molecular center, the four subunits of Kir6.2 form a canonical inward-rectifier K+ channel structure (Figures 1B and 2B).
evidence: Supported by structural analysis shown in Figures 1B and 2B

claim: The TMD0s are bound to the channel and hold the four ABC transporters akin to the leaves of a quatrefoil.
source: The TMD0s are bound to the channel and hold the four ABC transporters akin to the leaves of a quatrefoil.
evidence: Supported by structural analysis of cryo-EM data

claim: Residues 193–261, known as the L0-loop containing a conserved lasso motif, are not visible in the quatrefoil form.
source: EM density of the entire complex is very well defined, but residues 193–261, known as the L0-loop, containing a conserved lasso motif (Johnson and Chen, 2017; Li et al., 2017; Martin et al., 2017b; Zhang and Chen, 2016) is not visible (Figure 2).
evidence: Supported by cryo-EM density map analysis and citations to Johnson and Chen, 2017; Li et al., 2017; Martin et al., 2017b; Zhang and Chen, 2016

claim: The L0-loop is clearly visible in the propeller form.
source: In addition, the L0-loop is clearly visible in the propeller form albeit at lower resolution (Figure 1C and Figure 1—figure supplement 7).
evidence: Supported by cryo-EM density map shown in Figure 1C and Figure 1—figure supplement 7

claim: Each domain of the KATP maintains the same structure in both quatrefoil and propeller forms.
source: Each domain of the KATP maintains the same structure in both quatrefoil and propeller forms (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by structural comparison shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1

claim: The major difference between the quatrefoil and propeller forms lies in the different positions of the transporter module relative to the molecular center.
source: The major difference between the two structures lies in the different positions of the transporter module relative to the molecular center (Figure 1B and C; Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by structural comparison shown in Figure 1B and C; Figure 2—figure supplement 1

claim: The distance between the C-terminus of SUR1 and the first visible residue of Kir6.2 (Arg32) in the propeller form is 64.2 Å.
source: We further note that the distance between the C-terminus of SUR1 and the first visible residue of Kir6.2 (Arg32) in the propeller form is 64.2 Å, which is even greater than the corresponding distance in a recent propeller KATP structure without bound Mg2+-nucleotides (59.4 Å, PDB ID: 5TWV)(Martin et al., 2017b).
evidence: Supported by structural measurements and comparison with Martin et al., 2017b

claim: The corresponding distance between the C-terminus of SUR1 and Arg32 of Kir6.2 in a recent propeller KATP structure without bound Mg2+-nucleotides is 59.4 Å.
source: We further note that the distance between the C-terminus of SUR1 and the first visible residue of Kir6.2 (Arg32) in the propeller form is 64.2 Å, which is even greater than the corresponding distance in a recent propeller KATP structure without bound Mg2+-nucleotides (59.4 Å, PDB ID: 5TWV)(Martin et al., 2017b).
evidence: Supported by citation to Martin et al., 2017b and PDB ID: 5TWV

claim: The maximum distance spanned by the disordered region connecting the C-terminus of SUR1 and Kir6.2 Arg32 (37 a.a. total, including the (SA)3 linker) is 118.4 Å, assuming the Cα-Cα distance of adjacent residues in an extended strand spans 3.5 Å.
source: Assuming the Cα-Cα distance of adjacent residues in an extended strand spans 3.5 Å (Berg et al., 2002), the maximum distance spanned by the disordered region connecting the C-terminus of SUR1 and Kir6.2 Arg32 (37 a.a. total, including the (SA)3 linker) is 118.4 Å, which exceeds the observed distances mentioned above by ~2-fold.
evidence: Supported by calculation based on structural parameters from Berg et al., 2002

claim: The six-amino acid linker used in the KATPem construct is not expected to limit the range of motion sampled by SUR1 and Kir6.2 or introduce unnatural distortions to the propeller or quatrefoil forms.
source: Thus, we do not expect the six-amino acid linker used in the KATPem construct to limit the range of motion sampled by SUR1 and Kir6.2 or introduce unnatural distortions to the propeller or quatrefoil forms.
evidence: Based on inference from the distance calculations

claim: The fusion construct is functional and sensitive to nucleotides.
source: Moreover, the fusion construct is functional and sensitive to nucleotides (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1

claim: The transporter module of SUR1 resembles a canonical ABC transporter.
source: The transporter module of SUR1 resembles a canonical ABC transporter, TMD1 and TMD2 are domain-swapped, with TM9-10 from TMD1 and TM15-16 from TMD2 reaching across the interface between half-transporters to pack against the neighboring TMD (Figure 3A).
evidence: Supported by structural analysis shown in Figure 3A

claim: TMD1 and TMD2 of SUR1 are domain-swapped, with TM9-10 from TMD1 and TM15-16 from TMD2 reaching across the interface between half-transporters to pack against the neighboring TMD.
source: The transporter module of SUR1 resembles a canonical ABC transporter, TMD1 and TMD2 are domain-swapped, with TM9-10 from TMD1 and TM15-16 from TMD2 reaching across the interface between half-transporters to pack against the neighboring TMD (Figure 3A).
evidence: Supported by structural analysis shown in Figure 3A

claim: The NBDs of SUR1 dimerize in a head-to-tail fashion.
source: The NBDs dimerize in a head-to-tail fashion and nucleotides occupy both ATPase active sites at the dimer interface.
evidence: Supported by structural analysis

claim: Nucleotides occupy both ATPase active sites at the NBD dimer interface of SUR1.
source: The NBDs dimerize in a head-to-tail fashion and nucleotides occupy both ATPase active sites at the dimer interface.
evidence: Supported by structural analysis

claim: In the NBD-dimerized SUR1, a small cavity inside the TMDs is closed off from the extracellular milieu and remains accessible from the cytoplasm.
source: By contrast, in the NBD-dimerized SUR1, a small cavity inside the TMDs is closed off from the extracellular milieu and remains accessible from the cytoplasm (Figure 3A).
evidence: Supported by structural analysis shown in Figure 3A

claim: The structural features of SUR1 are consistent with SUR1 being a regulator of a K+ channel rather than a bona fide transporter itself.
source: These features are consistent with SUR1 being a regulator of a K+ channel rather than a bona fide transporter itself.
evidence: Based on inference from structural observations

claim: No substrate has been identified for SUR1.
source: This notion is further supported by the observation that no substrate has been identified for SUR1 hitherto (Aittoniemi et al., 2009; Schwappach et al., 2000).
evidence: Supported by citations to Aittoniemi et al., 2009; Schwappach et al., 2000

claim: The NBD dimer of SUR1 has an asymmetric configuration.
source: Another unusual feature of SUR1 is the asymmetric configuration of the NBD dimer.
evidence: Supported by structural analysis

claim: Mg2+-ATP is bound in the 'closed' catalytically inactive degenerate site of SUR1.
source: Mg2+-ATP is bound in the 'closed' catalytically inactive degenerate site and Mg2+-ADP is bound in the 'open' catalytically competent consensus ATPase site (Figure 3B–D, Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by structural analysis shown in Figure 3B–D, Figure 3—figure supplement 1

claim: Mg2+-ADP is bound in the 'open' catalytically competent consensus ATPase site of SUR1.
source: Mg2+-ATP is bound in the 'closed' catalytically inactive degenerate site and Mg2+-ADP is bound in the 'open' catalytically competent consensus ATPase site (Figure 3B–D, Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by structural analysis shown in Figure 3B–D, Figure 3—figure supplement 1

claim: SUR1 is the only ABC transporter observed with both Mg2+-ADP and Mg2+-ATP bound in its NBDs.
source: To our knowledge, this is the only ABC transporter observed with both Mg2+-ADP and Mg2+-ATP bound in its NBDs.
evidence: Based on comparison with known ABC transporter structures

claim: The structure of a dimeric ABC transporter, AaPrtD, shows Mg2+-ADP bound to both sites, but in this case both sites are the same and symmetrically closed around Mg2+-ADP.
source: We note that the structure of a dimeric ABC transporter, AaPrtD, shows Mg2+-ADP bound to both sites, but in this case both sites are the same and symmetrically closed around Mg2+-ADP (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by structural comparison shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2

claim: No ADP was added to the sample during structure determination of KATP.
source: In the structure determination of KATP, no ADP was added to the sample.
evidence: Describes the experimental conditions

claim: The degenerate ATP-binding site on SUR1 and the ATP inhibitory site on the channel are occupied by ATP.
source: While some ADP must have been generated through hydrolysis, it is clear that the degenerate ATP-binding site on SUR1 and the ATP inhibitory site on the channel are occupied by ATP.
evidence: Supported by structural analysis of nucleotide density

claim: The consensus site on SUR1, relative to the other ATP sites in the complex, is selective for ADP.
source: Thus, the consensus site on SUR1, relative to the other ATP sites in the complex, is selective for ADP (see below).
evidence: Based on inference from the observation that ADP occupies the consensus site while ATP occupies other sites

claim: The ATP turnover rate, expressed per SUR1 molecule, is approximately 0.02 per second.
source: We know from the rate of ATP hydrolysis (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C) that the ATP turnover rate, expressed per SUR1 molecule, is approximately 0.02 per second, which means the above reaction takes approximately 50 s to undergo a complete cycle.
evidence: Supported by ATPase activity measurements shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C

claim: The structure shows a relatively open cleft between bound ADP and solution in the consensus site of SUR1.
source: The structure shows a relatively open cleft between bound ADP and solution, therefore ADP dissociation is likely to be much faster than this slow turnover rate of 0.02 per second.
evidence: Supported by structural analysis

claim: ADP dissociation from the consensus site is likely to be much faster than the slow turnover rate of 0.02 per second.
source: The structure shows a relatively open cleft between bound ADP and solution, therefore ADP dissociation is likely to be much faster than this slow turnover rate of 0.02 per second.
evidence: Based on inference from structural observations

claim: The slow transition limiting the overall ATP hydrolysis rate is likely to be either the isomerization step from NBD open to NBD closed conformation (SATP ↔ S'ATP) or the hydrolysis step (S'ATP→ S'ADP + Pi).
source: A different transition must limit the overall rate. The slow transition is likely to be either the isomerization step from NBD open to NBD closed conformation (SATP ↔ S'ATP) or the hydrolysis step (S'ATP→ S'ADP + Pi).
evidence: Based on inference from kinetic analysis

claim: The occupancy of the consensus site by ADP must reflect equilibration of the site by ADP in solution through a rapid, reversible ADP dissociation reaction.
source: Base on this reasoning, the occupancy of S' by ADP must reflect equilibration of the site by ADP in solution (i.e. through a rapid, reversible ADP dissociation reaction, S'ADP ↔ S' + ADP).
evidence: Based on inference from kinetic reasoning

claim: Channel gating does not exhibit violation of microscopic reversibility.
source: The prior observation that channel gating does not exhibit violation of microscopic reversibility is also compatible with this assertion (Choi et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citation to Choi et al., 2008

claim: SUR1 is the target of sulphonylureas that inhibit KATP to promote insulin secretion.
source: SUR1 is the target of sulphonylureas that inhibit KATP to promote insulin secretion (Aguilar-Bryan et al., 1995; Ashcroft et al., 1987; Bryan et al., 2005; Dean and Matthews, 1968; Sturgess et al., 1985).
evidence: Supported by citations to Aguilar-Bryan et al., 1995; Ashcroft et al., 1987; Bryan et al., 2005; Dean and Matthews, 1968; Sturgess et al., 1985

claim: In a recent structure of the hamster-rat KATP hybrid, the glibenclamide-binding site was shown to reside within the TMDs of the inward-facing (i.e. NBD open) transporter module.
source: In a recent structure of the hamster-rat KATP hybrid, the glibenclamide-binding site was shown to reside within the TMDs of the inward-facing (i.e. NBD open) transporter module (Martin et al., 2017a)(Figure 3E).
evidence: Supported by citation to Martin et al., 2017a and shown in Figure 3E

claim: In the NBD-dimerized form, residues that comprise the glibenclamide-binding pocket move closer towards each other, making the cavity too small to accommodate glibenclamide.
source: In the NBD-dimerized form, residues that comprise the glibenclamide-binding pocket move closer towards each other, making the cavity too small to accommodate glibenclamide (Figure 3E).
evidence: Supported by structural comparison shown in Figure 3E

claim: Glibenclamide stabilizes the inward-facing conformation of SUR1.
source: This observation is entirely consistent with the hypothesis that glibenclamide stabilizes the inward-facing conformation (Martin et al., 2017a).
evidence: Supported by inference from structural observations and citation to Martin et al., 2017a

claim: Glibenclamide functions as a wedge to prevent adenosine nucleotide-mediated NBD closure and thus prevents SUR-mediated regulation of channel activity.
source: It functions as a wedge to prevent adenosine nucleotide-mediated NBD closure and thus prevents SUR-mediated regulation of channel activity.
evidence: Based on inference from structural observations

claim: Excellent side chain density is observed in both the pore and CTD of Kir6.2.
source: Excellent side chain density is observed in both the pore and CTD, which have allowed us to build most of the channel except for disordered flexible regions in the N- and C-termini of Kir6.2 (Figure 4B).
evidence: Supported by cryo-EM density map quality shown in Figure 4A and 4B

claim: Most of the Kir6.2 channel was built except for disordered flexible regions in the N- and C-termini.
source: Excellent side chain density is observed in both the pore and CTD, which have allowed us to build most of the channel except for disordered flexible regions in the N- and C-termini of Kir6.2 (Figure 4B).
evidence: Supported by model building from cryo-EM data

claim: The overall structure of human Kir6.2 is that of an inward-rectifier K+-channel with a large cytoplasmic domain.
source: The overall structure of human Kir6.2 is that of an inward-rectifier K+-channel with a large cytoplasmic domain.
evidence: Supported by structural analysis

claim: In the KATP structure, both the inner helix gate and the G-loop gates of Kir6.2 are closed.
source: In this structure, both the inner helix gate and the G-loop gates are closed (Figure 4B and Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by structural analysis shown in Figure 4B and Figure 4—figure supplement 1

claim: No PIP2 density was observed in the putative PIP2 binding sites even though C8-PIP2 was present in the sample.
source: No PIP2 density was observed in the putative PIP2 binding sites even though C8-PIP2 was present in the sample.
evidence: Supported by cryo-EM density map analysis

claim: PIP2 was present in Kir2 and GIRK inward rectifiers at similar concentrations.

evidence: Supported by citations to Edghill et al., 2010; Gloyn et al., 2004; Lang and Light, 2010; Proks et al., 2004

claim: Rotation of the transport module around the central axis of TMD0 (to convert from propeller to quatrefoil forms) can only occur if the lasso extension releases from its contact adjacent to the ATP site on the CTD.
